newsitem.title: BELARUS: President sacks Belarus "drunken" defence minister.
newsitem.headline: President sacks Belarus "drunken" defence minister.

text.p: Belarussian President Alexander Lukashenko, already locked in a constitutional row with a rebellious parliament, sacked his defence minister on Friday for turning up drunk at an official ceremony.
"The president took the decision in a specific situation in connection with the behaviour of Leonid Maltsev," presidential aide Vladimir Zametalin told Reuters.
Lukashenko had arrived with Maltsev at a ceremony to mark the 75th anniversary of a medical institute, where the minister was to deliver a welcoming address.
Maltsev mounted the podium and stumbled, "very drunk", through the start of his speech until Lukashenko interrupted him, a local journalist who gained access to the ceremony said.
"I apologise for the behaviour of the now former defence minister," Lukashenko was quoted as saying, after ordering Maltsev from the hall, accompanied by swarthy bodyguards.
State-owned television said Lukashenko had named as acting minister Lieutenant-General Alexander Chumakov, First Deputy Defence Minister and chief of the general staff.
Chumakov, seen by local observers as loyal to Lukashenko, is the fourth defence minister in five years.
A parallel controversy was meanwhile being played out in the constitutional court, trying to decide whether a referendum proposed for November 24 was legal.
Lukashenko is planning to use the referendum to extend his term by more than two years without elections and significantly broaden his authority over all branches of power.
Parliament has proposed its own referendum -- to ban the presidency outright and form a parliamentary democracy.
Each side accuses the other of ignoring Belarussian law by proposing new constitutions -- which cannot be put to a referendum -- rather than simple amendments, which can.
The court failed to decide who was in the right on Friday, adjourning until Monday after heated arguments put by advocates for each side.
Belarus, with 10 million inhabitants one of the former Soviet Union's smallest republics, has been no stranger to controversy since it received independence in 1991.
When a U.S. sports air balloon taking part in an international race entered Belarussian airspace last year, it was shot down by a fighter jet. Two American pilots were killed.
Lukashenko apologised to President Bill Clinton but then praised his 100,000-strong military for their battle-readiness.
The former collective farm chief has shown reluctance to cooperate with Western groups, and has accused foreign representatives of working for U.S. secret services.
Lukashenko won a landslide victory in July 1994 on a platform of fighting corruption and rebuilding ties between Russia and his country, sandwiched between Russia and Poland.
He has muzzled the press, banned independent trade unions and taken a tough line with his opponents -- so much so that two nationalist leaders won asylum in the United States this year.
